The core idea is to transform time series into time-frequency video tensors using the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), thereby preserving temporal dynamics while enabling the application of spatiotemporal models. The authors decompose each time series covariate into a trend component, extracted using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA), and a residual component, to which the STFT is applied. This transformation results in a video representation where the spatial dimensions correspond to frequency and covariates, and the temporal dimension represents the evolution of the time series. A custom video diffusion model is then trained on these video tensors to generate synthetic time series data. The model employs a transformer architecture with attention biases to capture spatiotemporal dependencies. The authors evaluate ST-Diff on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing time series generation methods, particularly in unconditional generation tasks. The empirical results suggest that the proposed time-series-as-video paradigm is a promising approach for capturing complex temporal and spectral dynamics in multivariate time series. The paper's main contribution lies in its innovative perspective of treating time series as videos, which allows for the utilization of advanced video diffusion techniques. The authors present a comprehensive evaluation, showcasing the effectiveness of their approach across various datasets. The results indicate that ST-Diff can generate high-fidelity and dynamically consistent time series, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The paper's significance lies in its potential to advance the field of time series generation by introducing a new perspective and demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. However, the paper also has limitations, particularly in its scope and lack of detailed analysis of computational complexity, which I will discuss in detail in the following sections.
